title: NIST SP 800-207 Zero Trust Architecture
hook: Never trust the network; verify every request to every resource.
summary: SP 800-207 defines zero trust architecture as a set of principles and logical components that remove implicit trust from the network. Access is granted per session based on identity, device posture, context and policy, with continuous monitoring.
keyPoints: Treat every data source and service as a resource, regardless of network location.
Secure all communication, internal or external, as if the network is hostile.
Grant access per session after dynamic policy evaluation; do not rely on static VPN trust.
Use a policy engine, policy administrator and policy enforcement points as the control plane.
Collect telemetry on identity, devices, traffic and behavior to improve decisions.
Micro-segmentation, software-defined perimeters and identity-aware proxies are key enablers.
Zero trust is an architecture journey, not a product category or a single purchase.
crownJewels: Crown-jewel applications and the data they expose.
Identities, device posture and the policy decision points.
Policy definitions, logs and continuous-monitoring telemetry.
Sensitive administrative interfaces and service accounts.
clientUse: Map the client's protect surface and prioritize the highest-value applications.
Define the policy engine and enforcement points before buying tools.
Sequence the journey around identity, device trust and micro-segmentation.
Measure reduced implicit trust and improved detection, not just tool deployment.

title: ISO/IEC 27017:2015 Cloud Security Controls
hook: Cloud-specific guidance for the shared-responsibility line.
summary: ISO/IEC 27017 gives cloud service customers and providers guidance on applying ISO/IEC 27002 controls in cloud environments. It clarifies who is responsible for what and adds controls for cloud-specific risks such as virtual environments and administrative access.
keyPoints: Distinguishes the responsibilities of cloud service customers and cloud service providers.
Adds cloud-specific controls and implementation guidance to the 27002 baseline.
Addresses shared infrastructure, virtualization, tenant separation and administrative access.
Covers asset ownership, data deletion, logging and monitoring in cloud services.
Helps define contract expectations and provider assurance questions.
It is a control guidance standard, not a certification scheme by itself.
crownJewels: Tenant data and workloads hosted in shared infrastructure.
Cloud provider and customer administrative credentials.
The virtualization layer and management plane.
Data deletion, backup and portability evidence.
Shared logs and monitoring data that cross responsibility boundaries.
clientUse: Clarify shared-responsibility splits before signing a cloud contract.
Assess provider controls against customer-side obligations and gaps.
Use it to extend an ISO 27001 ISMS into cloud services.
Build a provider-assurance questionnaire around the cloud-specific controls.

title: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1
hook: A cloud control library that maps the alphabet soup for you.
summary: The CSA Cloud Controls Matrix is a cloud-specific control framework with 197 control objectives across 17 domains. It maps controls to major standards, supports cloud assurance and underpins the CSA STAR programme.
keyPoints: 197 control objectives are organized into 17 security domains.
Controls cover governance, identity, data security, operations, resilience and third parties.
Cross-mappings reduce effort across ISO 27001, NIST, PCI DSS and other regimes.
The matrix supports both cloud service providers and cloud customers.
It is the control backbone of CSA STAR attestations and certifications.
Version 4.1 refines the v4 structure and keeps the cloud control language current.
crownJewels: Tenant data, identities and encryption keys.
Cloud management planes and APIs.
Logging, monitoring and incident evidence across shared infrastructure.
Supply-chain and sub-provider dependencies.
clientUse: Build a cloud control matrix and map it to the client's existing framework.
Assess providers consistently across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Use the mappings to avoid duplicated questionnaires and audits.
Anchor cloud assurance conversations around a shared vocabulary.

title: FedRAMP
hook: The gate for selling cloud services to the US federal government.
summary: FedRAMP authorizes cloud service offerings for federal use against NIST SP 800-53 baselines. It combines independent assessment, government authorization and continuous monitoring, with a modernization effort aimed at faster, reusable assurance.
keyPoints: Baselines include LI-SaaS, Low, Moderate and High, built on NIST SP 800-53.
An independent 3PAO assesses the provider; a government authorizing official makes the risk decision.
Authorization packages include the SSP, assessment report, POA&M and continuous-monitoring plan.
Agency authorizations and the FedRAMP marketplace support reuse across government.
Continuous monitoring requires monthly or annual evidence and timely incident reporting.
FedRAMP 20x is reshaping the programme around automation and continuous assurance.
crownJewels: Federal data and the systems that process it.
The authorization boundary, including inherited controls and dependencies.
Assessment evidence, POA&Ms and continuous-monitoring data.
Supply-chain provenance and personnel screening.
clientUse: Determine the correct impact baseline before scoping the assessment.
Build a control inheritance model with the cloud infrastructure provider.
Prepare evidence and automation for continuous monitoring from day one.
Use the marketplace and reuse patterns for faster agency authorization.

title: BSI Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue (C5)
hook: Germany's rigorous cloud audit standard, trusted across Europe.
summary: BSI C5 is a cloud-specific audit catalogue covering security, transparency and assurance. It is widely used by German and European customers to evaluate cloud providers, and can be attested by an independent auditor.
keyPoints: Covers governance, identity and access, encryption, operations, logging, procurement and compliance.
Requires transparency about the provider's security organization and control environment.
Independent auditors issue C5 attestation reports against the catalogue.
Addresses multi-tenancy, data location, portability and secure deletion.
Maps well to ISO 27001 but goes deeper on cloud-specific operational controls.
Version 2020 remains the reference; watch for newer BSI cloud guidance.
crownJewels: Customer data, metadata and encryption keys.
Multi-tenant isolation and administrative access.
Data location, deletion and portability controls.
Provider personnel, sub-processors and incident response.
clientUse: Use C5 attestations as a rigorous alternative to generic cloud questionnaires.
Map provider evidence to ISO 27001 and GDPR obligations.
Challenge scope, audit period and exceptions in the attestation.
Address data location and sub-processor risk for German clients.

title: ANSSI SecNumCloud
hook: France's sovereignty-focused qualification for trusted cloud providers.
summary: SecNumCloud is ANSSI's qualification scheme for cloud service providers that meet demanding security and sovereignty requirements. It is particularly relevant for French public-sector and critical-infrastructure customers handling sensitive data.
keyPoints: Covers governance, access control, encryption, resilience and supply-chain security.
Adds sovereignty criteria around control by non-EU actors and exposure to foreign law.
Qualification requires an audit and ongoing surveillance by ANSSI-accredited assessors.
Distinguishes different service models and deployment scopes.
Commonly requested for sensitive French public-sector and OIV work.
It is a qualification, not a generic ISO-style certification.
crownJewels: Sensitive and sovereign data hosted in the cloud.
Provider ownership, control and exposure to non-EU jurisdiction.
Encryption, key management and administrative access.
Supply-chain dependencies and provider exit capability.
clientUse: Assess sovereignty requirements before choosing a cloud provider.
Verify qualification scope and the services actually covered.
Use the referential to challenge provider control and sub-processor claims.
Plan an exit strategy that preserves data portability and service continuity.

title: CIS Benchmarks
hook: Prescriptive hardening settings for the platforms you actually run.
summary: CIS Benchmarks are consensus-developed hardening guides for cloud platforms, operating systems, databases, browsers and network devices. Each benchmark provides auditable settings at Level 1 and Level 2, with automated assessment options.
keyPoints: Benchmarks exist for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Windows, Linux, databases and network devices.
Level 1 is basic hygiene; Level 2 adds defense in depth for higher-risk environments.
Recommendations are specific, testable and mapped to CIS Controls.
CIS-CAT and third-party tools automate configuration assessment.
Organizations must tailor settings to operational requirements and document exceptions.
Drift is the enemy: benchmark once, then continuously verify.
crownJewels: Root and administrative accounts on every platform.
Logging, monitoring and audit trails.
Network exposure, identity configuration and encryption settings.
Operating-system and application hardening state.
Configuration drift and exception records.
clientUse: Select benchmarks for the actual platform estate, not the entire catalogue.
Use Level 1 for a defensible baseline; justify Level 2 deviations.
Automate assessment and feed drift into vulnerability management.
Document exceptions with owners, risk rationale and expiry dates.

title: OWASP Kubernetes Top 10
hook: The cluster misconfigurations attackers look for first.
summary: The OWASP Kubernetes Top 10 catalogues the most common security risks in Kubernetes environments. It focuses on misconfiguration, identity, supply chain and visibility gaps that turn a cluster into an attack path.
keyPoints: Insecure workload configurations expose secrets, host paths and privileged containers.
Supply-chain vulnerabilities enter through images, charts and third-party components.
Over-permissive RBAC and service accounts create lateral movement paths.
Missing network policies and segmentation allow unrestricted pod-to-pod traffic.
Secrets management, control-plane exposure and inadequate logging are recurring failures.
Admission control, policy-as-code and image signing are core mitigations.
crownJewels: Cluster control plane, API server and etcd.
Service accounts, tokens and workload identity.
Container images, registries and build pipelines.
Secrets, persistent volumes and tenant workloads.
Audit logs and runtime telemetry.
clientUse: Assess the cluster against the Top 10 before migrating production workloads.
Prioritize RBAC, network policy and admission control as structural fixes.
Integrate image scanning and signing into the build pipeline.
Use runtime detection to catch what configuration reviews miss.
